frameworks.name: Supply Chain Deconstraining Path
frameworks.definition: A three-lever sequence to unlock manufacturing-constrained growth: renegotiate payment terms, leverage influencer demand pull, and execute sell-outs to pull cash forward.

frameworks.name: Manufacturing Capital Acquisition Strategy
frameworks.definition: A path to own proprietary manufacturing equipment by achieving the manufacturer's volume capacity first, then purchasing the machine with cash generated by hitting that volume.

claims.text: A beef protein chip business doing $1M/year revenue remained supply-constrained for 6-9 months because changing product formulation away from commodity jerky dissuaded most manufacturers from bidding.
claims.speaker: Business Owner (Beef Protein Chips)

claims.text: Once a manufacturer was secured who can produce 20,000 units/month, the business can reach $280,000/month revenue with current product margins.
claims.speaker: Business Owner (Beef Protein Chips)

claims.text: The manufacturer's proprietary machine costs approximately $400,000 and can produce one tray of product every 12 seconds, but the equipment is too large for the current facility and requires either co-location or building a new facility.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi

claims.text: Renegotiating payment terms from net-zero to net-30, net-60, or longer dramatically accelerates cash flow; a portfolio company moved from net-zero to net-90 and grew from $2M/year to $5M/month in 18 months.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Extended payment terms defer cash outflow, allowing proceeds from current sales to fund next production batch without external capital.

claims.text: For the beef protein business, the primary demand-pull lever is influencer endorsement in the fitness space; the founder secured Austin Hatfield, a high-probability CrossFit Games podium finisher, as the primary influencer and is allocating all inventory into that channel rather than running paid ads.
claims.speaker: Business Owner (Beef Protein Chips)

claims.text: Selling out of inventory and using pre-orders are mechanisms to pull cash forward and create pent-up demand that can fuel the next production cycle without requiring external capital.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Ability to fulfill pre-orders in reasonable timeframe
claims.mechanism: Selling out creates urgency and signals scarcity; pre-orders pull cash 30-90 days ahead of production.
bounded_by: Does not work if product demand is weak
Does not work if fulfillment delays erode trust

claims.text: The owner previously executed a sell-out play to manage a supplier change; when switching manufacturers with limited time to produce, the team rented equipment and solved production in real-time to fulfill orders.
claims.speaker: Business Owner (Beef Protein Chips)

claims.text: If the business scales to hit the new manufacturer's capacity (20,000 units/month) using extended payment terms, pre-orders, and influencer demand-pull, the owner can accumulate sufficient cash to purchase the proprietary machine ($400,000) without external financing.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Payment terms extended to net-30 or longer
claims.mechanism: Extended terms defer outflow, pre-orders pull inflow forward, and volume scales unit profit—three concurrent levers accumulate cash faster than debt service costs.

claims.text: The proprietary production machine is the core defensibility of the business; understanding exactly how the machine works and its actual build cost is critical before scaling because the machine is the primary differentiation from commodity competitors.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Machine defensibility compounds: scaling requires more machines, and knowing how they work enables rapid replication without vendor lock-in.
bounded_by: Does not apply to service or software businesses

claims.text: The manufacturer may be significantly marking up the proprietary machine cost; one comparable machine-building company sells machinery at $400,000 average price but costs them only $17,000 to build, suggesting a 23x markup.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
bounded_by: Actual proprietary cost unknown without inspection

claims.text: The business owner should inspect the proprietary machine with a qualified engineer before committing to the $400,000 purchase to verify actual bill-of-materials cost and assess whether the markup is justified.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi

examples.text: A portfolio company extended manufacturer payment terms from net-zero (immediate payment) to net-90 (payment due in 90 days) through direct negotiation. With cash flow unlocked by delayed payment, the company grew from $2M in annual revenue to $5M in monthly revenue within 18 months.

The beef protein business owner switched manufacturers due to QA failures and late deliveries. Rather than pause sales, the team rented equipment, solved production in real-time, and executed a sell-out play to clear orders. This demonstrated that supply emergencies can be solved operationally when demand is present.

A machine-building company with $70M in annual revenue sells machinery at $400,000 average price, but the actual manufacturing cost is only $17,000 per machine, representing a 23x markup. This illustrates that custom/proprietary machinery is often vastly over-priced relative to actual build cost.

practices.text: When supply-constrained, prioritize renegotiating payment terms with your manufacturer as the first lever before pursuing price increases or demand generation.
Use sell-outs and pre-orders as mechanisms to pull cash forward and create pent-up demand that can be fulfilled by the next production cycle.
Before purchasing proprietary manufacturing equipment, inspect it with a qualified engineer and understand its actual bill-of-materials cost to assess markup and avoid overpaying.
If owning manufacturing is a long-term strategy for defensibility, invest in understanding how proprietary equipment works so you can scale or replicate it without vendor dependency.
